newsitem.title: USA: MFA calls CFTC Internet interpretation unfair.
newsitem.headline: MFA calls CFTC Internet interpretation unfair.

text.p: The Managed Futures Association said the Commodity Futures Trading Commission's stance on electronic dissemination of trading information was unfair, and it urged industry professionals to voice their concerns to the CFTC.
The MFA, an industry group, wrote to the CFTC this week protesting the commission's view of disclosure documents on Websites of commodity trading advisers (CTAs) and commodity pool operators.
Industry professionals have until November 14 to respond to the CFTC's proposed interpretation of the Commodity Exchange Act.

The CFTC would require potential investors surfing the Internet to scroll through a lengthy disclosure document before accessing a Website, where they could find a CTA's statement of recent performance, trading philosophy and amount of money under management.
The MFA thinks the disclosure document should be available to click on and read, but that scrolling through the document in its entirety should not be needed just to enter the Website.
"You need a host of patience to go through what they're requiring," John Gaine, MFA general counsel and director of government relations, said in an interview on Friday.

Futures professionals at the Futures Industry Association exposition here this week said the CFTC's interpretation could become an unnecessary hurdle to attracting potential investors on the Internet.
"Regulation should be the same between traditional paper media and the Internet," said Paula Pierce, futures industry attorney and MFA board member, in a technology panel discussion on Thursday.

She noted that CTAs can send solicitation materials through the mail and include a disclosure document, but cannot force a potential investor to page through it. The investor has the option to set it aside, read it later, or ignore it.

Another issue, Pierce said, is that potential investors can pick up any number of industry publications to find the same sort of information found on a CTA's Website, all without reading a disclosure document.
MFA Chairman John Frawley and other industry professionals said they stood behind disclosure documents and encouraged investors to read them.
But many said the CFTC's interpretation was more strict for the electronic media than for traditional print media.
"You still need customer protection (with a disclosure document), but this is like starting a high hurdle race with shackles on your legs and a ball dragging behind you," Gaine said.
